title: Atomic Structure and Radioactivity
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Atomic Structure and Radioactivity Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_text: The structure of an atom and the nuclear model; isotopes; the development of the model of the atom; radioactive decay and nuclear radiation: alpha, beta and gamma; nuclear equations; half-lives and the random nature of radioactive decay; radioactive contamination and irradiation; background radiation and the hazards and uses of nuclear radiation.
meta_desc: Free Year 10 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on radioactivity: alpha, beta and gamma radiation, nuclear equations, half-life, activity, contamination and irradiation, and background radiation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay.
key_sub: Alpha is most ionising; gamma is most penetrating.
body_html:
How to think about it

Unstable nuclei decay randomly, giving out radiation.

  • Alpha (helium nucleus): stopped by paper, strongly ionising. Beta (electron): stopped by aluminium. Gamma (EM wave): reduced by thick lead.
  • Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta decay: atomic number +1.
  • Half-life: the time for the count rate (or number of nuclei) to halve.
Example

800 counts, half-life 2 h. After 6 h?

3 half-lives

800 → 400 → 200 → 100

Answer: 100

Example

²³⁸U emits alpha. New mass number?

238 − 4

Answer: 234

Common mistakes

  • Thinking gamma is the most ionising.
  • Thinking irradiated objects become radioactive.
  • Thinking half-life is half the time for all of it to decay.

faq.q: What are alpha, beta and gamma radiation?
faq.a: Alpha particles are helium nuclei, beta particles are fast electrons from the nucleus, and gamma rays are electromagnetic waves.
The time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample, or its count rate, to halve.

faq.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
faq.a: Irradiation is being exposed to radiation from outside; contamination is radioactive atoms getting onto or into something. Irradiated objects do not become radioactive.

items.q: What is activity?
c: the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerels (Bq)
the energy of an alpha particle
items.e: 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.

items.q: What does 'random' mean for radioactive decay?
c: You cannot predict which nucleus will decay next or when.
It can be stopped by cooling.
Every nucleus decays at the same time.
items.e: Only the overall pattern is predictable.

stopped by a few mm of aluminium
items.e: Alpha: most ionising, least penetrating. Gamma: least ionising, most penetrating.
